stages.title: Language sounds and pronunciation
stages.hook: Say 'pão' (bread) and 'mão' (hand). Does the sound come partly through your nose?
explain: Portuguese has nasal vowels. The mark ~ (til) or an m or n after a vowel makes the sound go through the nose: pão (bread), mão (hand), mãe (mother), limão (lemon), bom (good). The ending -ão is one of the most typical sounds of the language.

Other special sounds: nh is like ny in canyon (banho, bath); lh is like lli in million (filho, son); ch is like sh (chave, key); ç is like s (coração, heart). In Brazil, the letter r at the start of a word (rua, street) sounds like an English h. In many Brazilian accents t and d before i sound like ch and j (dia, day).
stages.mnemonic: Say 'pão' and hold your nose: the sound still comes out through it.

gq.q: What does the til (~) in 'mão' show?
o: The stress is on the first syllable
gq.why: The til marks a nasal vowel.
Nh is a palatal nasal, like Spanish ñ.

panel.q: A learner says 'filho' as 'fil-ho' with a clear l and h. What is the usual sound of lh?
panel.why: Lh is a palatal l, as in million.

panel.q: Why does 'coração' have a cedilla (ç)?
o: So that c sounds like k
So that c is pronounced like s before a
panel.why: Ç gives an s sound before a, o, u.

panel.q: In Brazil, how is the first r of 'rua' typically pronounced?
o: Like a Spanish rolled r in all accents
panel.why: Brazilian initial r is often a breathy h sound.

teach.model: Portuguese has nasal vowels like pão and mão. Nh is like ny, lh is like lli in million, ch is sh, and ç is s. Brazilian initial r sounds like h.

points.ask: How do nh and lh sound?

trip.prompt: Listen for nasal vowels in the examples.

stages.title: Alphabet, script or basic characters
stages.hook: Portuguese letters have little marks over them. Why?
explain: Portuguese uses the Latin alphabet. Since the 2009 Orthographic Agreement the alphabet officially has 26 letters, including k, w and y, though these are mainly used in foreign words and names. Marks over letters (diacritics) matter: acute á é í ó ú (open or stressed sounds), circumflex â ê ô (closed sounds), grave à (a contraction), tilde ã õ (nasal) and cedilla ç.

A mark can change the word: avô (grandfather) and avó (grandmother) differ only in the accent. There is no ñ in Portuguese. Capital letters are used for names and at the start of sentences, but not for days, months or languages: segunda-feira, janeiro, português.
stages.mnemonic: One mark can turn grandpa into grandma: avô, avó.

gq.q: Which words differ only by an accent?
gq.why: Avô is grandfather and avó is grandmother.

gq.q: Are days and months capitalised in Portuguese?
o: No, they start with lower case
gq.why: Portuguese writes segunda-feira and janeiro in lower case.

panel.q: Why does 'avó' need the accent?
o: It distinguishes it from avô and shows the open o
panel.why: The acute and circumflex give different words.

panel.q: Which letter is not used in Portuguese?
panel.why: Portuguese has ç and ã but no ñ.

panel.q: Why were k, w and y formally added in 2009?
o: Because they appear in foreign words and names
Because they are common in native words
panel.why: The agreement listed all 26 letters.

teach.model: Portuguese uses 26 Latin letters plus accents: á é í ó ú, â ê ô, ã õ, à and ç. Accents can change meaning, such as avô and avó.

points.ask: What is an example of an accent changing meaning?

trip.prompt: Find the accent marks and what they do.

stages.title: Greetings and introductions
stages.hook: What do you say when you meet someone in Brazil and in Portugal?
explain: Basic greetings: Olá or Oi (Hi, Oi is very common in Brazil), Bom dia (good morning), Boa tarde (good afternoon), Boa noite (good evening or good night). To ask 'How are you?': Tudo bem? (Brazil and Portugal) or Como vai? In Brazil people also say Como você está?; in Portugal Como está? or, with friends, Como estás?

Say your name with 'Meu nome é ...' or 'Me chamo ...' (Brazil); in Portugal 'Chamo-me ...'. Reply to an introduction with 'Prazer!' or 'Muito prazer!' (Nice to meet you). To thank: men say 'obrigado', women say 'obrigada'. To say goodbye: Tchau, Até logo (see you later), Até amanhã (see you tomorrow).
stages.mnemonic: Oi in Brazil, Olá everywhere; obrigado for boys, obrigada for girls.

gq.q: A woman wants to say thank you. Which word does she use?
gq.why: Obrigado agrees with the speaker's gender, so women say obrigada.

gq.q: Which greeting is used at about 3 pm?

panel.q: In Portugal a person says 'Chamo-me João'. What is different from Brazil?
o: The pronoun me is placed after the verb
panel.why: European Portuguese puts the clitic pronoun after the verb in this case: Chamo-me; Brazil prefers Me chamo.

panel.q: Why is 'Tudo bem?' so useful?
o: It is both a question and an answer
panel.why: Tudo bem? can be asked and answered with Tudo bem!

panel.q: Which phrase is used as 'See you tomorrow'?
panel.why: Amanhã means tomorrow.

teach.model: Say Oi or Olá, Bom dia, Boa tarde, Boa noite. Ask Tudo bem? Say Meu nome é... or Me chamo... (Brazil) or Chamo-me... (Portugal). Obrigado/a agrees with the speaker.

points.ask: How do I say my name?
How do I say thank you?

trip.prompt: Compare greetings used in Brazil and Portugal.

stages.title: Numbers and counting
stages.hook: How many numbers can you say from one to ten in Portuguese?
explain: The numbers from one to ten are um, dois, três, quatro, cinco, seis, sete, oito, nove, dez. Um and dois change with gender: um livro (one book, masculine), uma caneta (one pen, feminine); dois livros, duas canetas.

Higher numbers: onze (11), doze (12), vinte (20), trinta (30), cem (100). Numbers go before the noun and the noun is plural: três livros. In writing, use the plural -s: cinco gatos. Telephone numbers are usually said digit by digit or in pairs.
stages.mnemonic: Um livro, uma caneta: the number matches the thing.
sentences: There are five books on the table.

gq.why: Caneta is feminine, so it takes duas and the plural -s.

panel.q: Why is it 'dois livros' but 'duas casas'?
o: Dois is masculine and duas is feminine
panel.why: Um and dois agree with gender.

panel.q: After a number, is the Portuguese noun singular or plural?
panel.why: Portuguese nouns take plural after numbers above one.

panel.q: Which is correct for 'one house'?
panel.why: Casa is feminine.

teach.model: Count um, dois, três, quatro, cinco, seis, sete, oito, nove, dez. Um and dois change with gender: um livro, uma casa, dois livros, duas casas. Nouns become plural after numbers above one.

stages.title: Colours and shapes
stages.hook: Which colours are on the Brazilian flag? And is the green the same as on the Portuguese flag?
explain: Colours: vermelho (red), azul (blue), verde (green), amarelo (yellow), preto (black), branco (white), laranja (orange), rosa (pink). Colours usually come after the noun and agree with it: uma casa vermelha, dois carros vermelhos. Laranja and rosa often do not change.

Shapes: círculo, quadrado, triângulo, retângulo. The Brazilian flag is green, yellow, blue and white: verde e amarelo are national colours. The Portuguese flag is green and red (verde e vermelho). Colour words are adjectives, so they agree in gender and number.
stages.mnemonic: After the noun, same gender and number: gato preto, gata preta.

gq.q: How do you say 'a red house'?
gq.why: Casa is feminine, so the adjective is vermelha and comes after.

gq.q: Which colours are national colours of Brazil?

panel.q: Why is it 'carros vermelhos' and not 'carros vermelho'?
panel.why: Adjectives take the plural -s with the noun.

panel.q: Where does the colour usually go?
o: At the end of the sentence
panel.why: Most adjectives follow the noun in Portuguese.

panel.q: Which shows agreement correctly?
panel.why: Gata is feminine so preta.

teach.model: Colours follow the noun and agree with it: uma casa vermelha, dois carros vermelhos. Shapes: círculo, quadrado, triângulo.

trip.prompt: Compare the colours of the flags of Brazil and Portugal.

stages.title: Family and people
stages.hook: How do you say 'my mother' and 'my father' in Portuguese?
explain: Family words: mãe (mother), pai (father), irmão (brother), irmã (sister), avô (grandfather), avó (grandmother), tio (uncle), tia (aunt), filho (son), filha (daughter). 'Meus pais' means 'my parents' (and also 'my mother and father').

Possessives: meu/minha (my), seu/sua (your, his/her), nosso/nossa (our). They agree with the thing owned, not the owner: minha mãe, meu pai. In Brazil people usually say 'minha mãe'; in Portugal the article is common: 'a minha mãe'. Family is very important in all Lusophone cultures.
stages.mnemonic: Meu pai, minha mãe: the word follows the person owned.

gq.why: Pais means parents; pães is breads.

panel.q: Why is it 'minha mãe' and not 'meu mãe'?
o: The possessive agrees with mãe, which is feminine
panel.why: Possessives agree with the noun.

panel.q: How does Portugal differ from Brazil with possessives?
o: Portugal usually adds the article: a minha mãe
panel.why: European Portuguese usually includes the article.

panel.q: What does 'os irmãos' mean?
panel.why: The masculine plural also covers mixed groups.

teach.model: Use mãe, pai, irmão, irmã, avô, avó. Possessives agree with the noun: meu pai, minha mãe. Portugal often adds the article.

stages.title: Common objects
stages.hook: Is 'a mesa' feminine or masculine? And what do you call a mobile phone?
explain: Every Portuguese noun has a gender. Feminine nouns usually end in -a and use a (the) or uma (a): a mesa (the table), a porta (the door), a janela (the window). Masculine nouns usually end in -o and use o or um: o copo (the glass), o livro (the book). Plural: add -s.

Words differ in Brazil and Portugal: celular in Brazil, telemóvel in Portugal (mobile phone); ônibus (Brazil) and autocarro (Portugal) for bus. Other objects: cadeira (chair), mala (suitcase), chave (key). Use 'Isto é ...' (This is ...) or 'O que é isto?' (What is this?).
stages.mnemonic: A mesa, o copo: a goes with -a, o goes with -o.
sentences: The glass is on the table.

gq.q: How do Brazilians usually say 'mobile phone'?
gq.why: Celular in Brazil, telemóvel in Portugal.

panel.q: Why do learners need to learn the article with the noun?
o: Gender is the same for all nouns
panel.why: Some nouns break the -o/-a pattern, such as o dia.

panel.q: What is the plural of 'copo'?
panel.why: Add -s to nouns ending in a vowel.

panel.q: Which phrase asks 'What is this?'
panel.why: O que means what.

teach.model: Every noun has a gender: a mesa, o copo. Add -s for plural. Words differ: celular (Brazil), telemóvel (Portugal).

points.ask: How do I make a plural?
What differs in Brazil and Portugal?

stages.title: Everyday actions
stages.hook: How do you say 'I eat', 'I drink' and 'I run' in Portuguese?
explain: Portuguese verbs end in -ar, -er or -ir: falar (to speak), comer (to eat), dormir (to sleep), beber (to drink), correr (to run), ir (to go), ler (to read), escrever (to write). In the present, the ending shows the person: eu falo, eu como, eu durmo.

For 'we', the endings are -amos, -emos, -imos: nós falamos, nós comemos, nós dormimos. The subject pronoun is often dropped: 'Como pão' means 'I eat bread'. Brazil often uses 'você' for 'you': você fala, with the same ending as he or she (ele/ela fala).
stages.mnemonic: Falo, como, durmo: the ending o means I.

gq.q: What ending shows 'I' in the present?
gq.why: Eu falo, eu como, eu durmo.

panel.q: Why can Portuguese say 'Como pão' without 'eu'?
panel.why: Verb endings identify the person.

panel.q: How do you say 'we speak'?
panel.why: The -amos ending is for we.

panel.q: In Brazil, which pronoun is commonly used for 'you'?
panel.why: Você is common in most of Brazil.

teach.model: Verbs end in -ar, -er, -ir. Present endings include -o for eu and -amos/-emos/-imos for nós. The subject pronoun can be dropped.

stages.title: Simple listening and speaking
stages.hook: You did not understand a sentence in Portuguese. What can you say?
explain: Useful phrases: 'Pode repetir, por favor?' (Can you repeat, please?), 'Fale mais devagar, por favor' (Speak more slowly, please), 'Não entendi' (I did not understand), 'Como se diz ... em português?' (How do you say ... in Portuguese?), 'Desculpe' (Sorry, excuse me).

When listening, catch key words and numbers. Portuguese is spoken quite fast and the unstressed vowels are weak, especially in Portugal. Brazilian speech is often described as more open and clear. To speak: say the words slowly, make the nasal sounds clear, and use gestures. Mistakes are normal.
stages.mnemonic: Pode repetir? Fale mais devagar. Não entendi.

gq.why: Entendi is I understood; não negates.

gq.q: Which phrase is polite for asking someone to slow down?

panel.q: Why add 'por favor' to requests?
panel.why: Por favor means please.

panel.q: Where does the word 'não' go in 'Eu não entendi'?
o: At the start of the sentence
panel.why: Portuguese places não before the verb.

panel.q: Which question asks how to say a word?
panel.why: Como se diz asks for a translation.

teach.model: Use Pode repetir, por favor?, Fale mais devagar and Não entendi. Add por favor. Não goes before the verb.

points.ask: How do I ask to repeat?
How do I ask to slow down?
How do I say I did not understand?
